solution:
**Carbon (C).**

Section 9.3 describes group 14 as the one group in which all three traditional types of element occur together: *carbon is a nonmetal, silicon is a metalloid which is brittle like nonmetal, it is hard and has metallic luster. Germanium is also brittle but hard and lustrous metalloid. Tin or lead down the group are corrosion resistant and moderately reactive.* Carbon is therefore the only member of group 14 the chapter calls a nonmetal; Si and Ge are metalloids and Sn and Pb are metals.

**Carbon (C)** — it forms \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), the most acidic oxide of group 14.

Section 9.4.3 states that the increase in metallic character down groups 13, 14 and 15 is reflected in their oxides, which *gradually vary from acidic through amphoteric to basic*. Table 9.6 shows this for group 14: \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) acidic, \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) acidic, \(\mathrm{GeO_2}\) acidic, \(\mathrm{SnO_2}\) amphoteric and \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\) amphoteric. Acidic character is therefore greatest at the top of the group, and carbon — the least metallic and most electronegative member (electronegativity 2.5 in Table 9.3, the highest in the group) — forms the most acidic oxide.

**Lead (Pb).**

Table 9.5 gives the group oxidation state of group 14 as \(+4\), with \(+2\) and \(-4\) as the other states, and section 9.4.1 states that the lower oxidation states *become increasingly stable as we move down to heavier elements in the groups*, an effect the 'Remember' box attributes to the inert pair effect. Lead is the heaviest member of group 14, so its \(+2\) state is the most stable of the group. The worked example on \(\mathrm{GeCl_4}\) and \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) settles it directly: *the stability of the oxidation state 2 is more in Pb than in Ge*, which is why Table 9.5 lists \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) rather than \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\) among the stable compounds.

**Carbon (C).**

Carbon is the only member of group 14 the chapter shows forming \(\pi\) bonds. Section 9.6.1 describes graphite as hexagonal nets of \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) carbons, each bonded to three neighbours by sigma bonds, and states that *the fourth electron is in the unhybrid p-orbital of each carbon. The p-orbitals on all the carbons are parallel to each other. These overlap laterally to form \(\pi\) bonds.* Table 9.5 likewise lists \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), in which carbon is doubly bonded to each oxygen, among the stable compounds of the group.

Carbon can do this because it is the smallest atom in group 14 — Table 9.3 gives its atomic radius as 77 pm against silicon's 118 pm. Sideways overlap of p orbitals needs the two atoms close together, and that overlap becomes weak once the atoms are as large as silicon and below. That is also why the heavier members prefer network structures held by single bonds: section 9.7.5 describes silica not as discrete \(\mathrm{O=Si=O}\) molecules but as a three dimensional network in which each silicon is singly bonded to four oxygen atoms.

(The chapter does not compare \(\pi\)-bond strengths across group 14 in so many words; the answer follows from the \(\pi\) bonding it describes for carbon in graphite together with the atomic radii of Table 9.3.)

[Textbook misprint: the question as printed asks why \(\mathrm{Ga^{3\oplus}}\) salts are the better reducing agent. \(\mathrm{Ga^{3\oplus}}\) is gallium in its highest and, for a light group 13 element, most stable oxidation state; it cannot be oxidised further and so cannot act as a reducing agent. On the chapter's own inert-pair reasoning the reducing species is gallium in the \(+1\) state, which is readily oxidised to the stable \(+3\) state. The stem is transcribed as printed and the contrast the question is drawing is answered above.]

The comparison rests on the inert pair effect described in section 9.4.1 and its 'Remember' box: in the heavier p-block elements the oxidation state two units below the group value becomes increasingly stable, because the valence s-electrons are shielded poorly by the ten inner d-electrons and so take part less readily in bonding.

Gallium is the period-4 member of group 13, and for it the group oxidation state \(+3\) is the stable one, while the \(+1\) state is not. A gallium species in the \(+1\) state therefore gives up its two s-electrons readily to reach the stable \(+3\) state — that is, it is oxidised easily — and so acts as a **reducing agent**.

Thallium is the heaviest member of the same group, and there the inert pair effect makes \(+1\) the stable state, as the worked example on \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 1}}\) versus \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 3}}\) concludes. A \(\mathrm{Tl^{3\oplus}}\) salt therefore accepts two electrons readily to fall to the stable \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 1}}\) state — it is reduced easily — and so acts as an **oxidising agent**.

Lead is the heaviest member of group 14, lying in period 6. Table 9.5 gives \(+4\) as the group oxidation state of group 14 and \(+2\) as the other state, and section 9.4.1 states that the lower oxidation state becomes increasingly stable as we move down to the heavier elements of a group. The 'Remember' box gives the cause: in these heavy elements the two valence s-electrons are shielded poorly by the ten inner d-electrons, are held more tightly by the nucleus, and so are involved less readily in chemical reactions — the **inert pair effect**.

In \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\) lead uses all four valence electrons and is in the \(+4\) state; in \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) it uses only its two p-electrons and retains the inert s-pair, giving the \(+2\) state. Because the inert pair effect is strong in lead, the \(+2\) state is the more stable of the two and \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) is accordingly the more stable chloride — which is why Table 9.5 lists \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\), not \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\), among the stable compounds of group 14. The worked example on \(\mathrm{GeCl_4}\) and \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) makes the same point: the stability of the \(+2\) state is greater in Pb than in Ge.

**\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)** (carbon dioxide) — listed in Table 9.5 among the stable compounds of group 14.

Oxygen is assigned \(-2\), so if \(x\) is the oxidation state of carbon, \(x + 2(-2) = 0\), giving \(x = +4\). This is the group oxidation state of group 14, which Table 9.5 gives as \(+4\).

\(\mathrm{CCl_4}\), also listed in Table 9.5, is an equally acceptable answer: chlorine is \(-1\), so \(x + 4(-1) = 0\) and \(x = +4\).

**\(\mathrm{CO}\)** (carbon monoxide).

Section 9.4.3 states that the elements of group 14 on heating in air or oxygen form oxides of the type EO and \(\mathrm{EO_2}\), *in accordance with the stable oxidation state and availability of oxygen* :

\(\mathrm{E(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{EO}\)

For \(\mathrm{E = C}\) this is carbon monoxide. Taking oxygen as \(-2\), \(x + (-2) = 0\), so carbon is in the \(+2\) state — the 'other oxidation state' Table 9.5 lists for group 14, two units below the group value.

**\(\mathrm{CH_4}\)** (methane) — listed in Table 9.5 among the stable compounds of group 14.

Carbon is more electronegative than hydrogen (Table 9.3 gives carbon 2.5, the highest in the group), so in a C-H bond the shared pair is assigned to carbon and each hydrogen counts as \(+1\). Hence \(x + 4(+1) = 0\), giving \(x = -4\), the negative oxidation state Table 9.5 lists for group 14.

The atomic radii of group 13, from Table 9.2, are B 88 pm, Al 143 pm, Ga 135 pm, In 167 pm and Tl 170 pm.

**Overall trend :** the radius increases down the group, because each successive element adds a new shell, so the outermost electrons lie further from the nucleus and are better screened from it.

**The anomaly at gallium :** gallium is *smaller* than aluminium (135 pm against 143 pm), against the general trend. The worked example in section 9.3 gives the reason. Aluminium has no d-electrons; going from Al to Ga the nuclear charge increases by 18 units, and of the 18 electrons added, ten enter the inner 3d subshell. d-Electrons shield poorly, so the outer electrons of gallium feel the increased nuclear charge much more strongly than the extra shell relaxes it, and the atom contracts. Beyond gallium the normal increase resumes, In (167 pm) and Tl (170 pm) being larger again.

The first ionization enthalpies of group 13, from Table 9.2, are B 801, Al 577, Ga 579, In 558 and Tl 589 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

**Overall trend :** section 9.4.2 states that *as we move down the group, the ionization enthalpies are lowered*, because the atomic radii increase — the valence shell orbitals become more diffuse — so the outermost electron is held less tightly and is easier to remove. The large fall from boron to aluminium, 801 to 577 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), is this effect.

**Below aluminium the fall stops :** from Al onwards the values stay close together and are irregular, Ga (579) and Tl (589) being slightly *higher* than the element above each. The cause is the same one the worked example in section 9.3 uses for the atomic radii: the ten inner d-electrons that first appear at gallium, and the fourteen f-electrons that additionally appear at thallium, shield the nucleus poorly, so the increased nuclear charge is felt strongly by the valence electron and holds it more tightly than the extra shell alone would suggest.

**The chapter does not state this.** Table 9.2, which carries the atomic and physical properties of the group 13 elements, lists atomic number, atomic mass, atomic radius, ionic radius, the first three ionization enthalpies, electronegativity, density, melting point and boiling point — but **no electron-affinity values**, and the phrase 'electron affinity' occurs nowhere in the body of this chapter. So no trend in electron affinity can be read off the chapter's own data.

What the chapter does supply, and what the trend follows from, is the size trend of Table 9.2. Electron affinity is the energy change on adding an electron to a gaseous atom; the larger the atom, the further the incoming electron sits from the nucleus and the less strongly it is attracted, so the electron affinity falls in magnitude down a group. Boron is the exception in the other direction: it is so small (88 pm) that the added electron enters a compact 2p shell where inter-electronic repulsion is severe, so boron's electron affinity is *lower* in magnitude than aluminium's. Beyond aluminium the magnitude then decreases down the group as the atoms enlarge.

This last paragraph goes beyond what the chapter prints and should be treated as background rather than as a result derived from it.

**\(\mathrm{sp^2}\).**

Section 9.7.2 states it directly: *Aluminium atom in aluminium chloride is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised, with one vacant unhybrid p orbital.* The three \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybrid orbitals are used for the three Al-Cl bonds, which makes the \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) unit trigonal planar, and the vacant unhybridised p orbital is what allows two such units to join into the dimer \(\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}\) by accepting a lone pair from a chlorine atom of the other unit.

**Diborane, \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\).**

Section 9.7.4 describes it: in diborane the 1s orbital of each of two hydrogen atoms overlaps simultaneously with a half-filled \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybrid orbital of one boron atom and the vacant \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybrid orbital of the other. *This type of overlap produces two three centred - two electron bonds (3 c - 2e) or **banana bonds**.* The two hydrogen atoms taking part in them are the bridging H atoms, and they lie symmetrically above and below the plane containing the two boron atoms and the four terminal hydrogen atoms.

Orthophosphoric acid is \(\mathrm{H_3PO_4}\). Section 9.7.7 states that it *contains three ionizable acidic hydrogens* and that *the central phosphorous atom is tetrahedral*.

So phosphorus sits at the centre of a tetrahedron. It is joined to four oxygen atoms: one by a double bond \(\mathrm{(P=O)}\), and three by single bonds, each of those three oxygens carrying a hydrogen atom as an \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group. Written linearly the molecule is \(\mathrm{O=P(OH)_3}\), and it is the three \(\mathrm{-OH}\) hydrogens that are the ionizable acidic hydrogens — which is why the acid is tribasic.

The structure as the chapter draws it is shown with this answer.

Nitric acid is \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\). Section 9.7.6 states that *the central nitrogen atom is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised* and that \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) *exhibits resonance phenomenon*.

The nitrogen is bonded to three oxygen atoms: one through the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group and two others. Those last two are **not** distinguishable in the real molecule: two contributing structures can be written, one with the double bond to the first of them and the negative charge on the second, and one with the double bond and the charge interchanged. Nitrogen carries a positive formal charge in both. The true molecule is the resonance hybrid of the two, in which each of the two nitrogen-oxygen bonds is identical and carries a partial negative charge \(\delta^{\ominus}\).

The chapter's own figure gives the dimensions of that hybrid: the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond length 96 pm, the \(\mathrm{N-O}\) bond length 140.6 pm, the \(\mathrm{H-O-N}\) angle \(120^\circ\) and the \(\mathrm{O-N-O}\) angle \(130^\circ\).

The two resonance structures and the resonance hybrid, as the chapter draws them, are shown with this answer.

Both are allotropes of carbon, described in section 9.6.1.

| | Diamond | Graphite |
|---|---|---|
| Hybridisation of carbon | \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) | \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) |
| Bonding to neighbours | each carbon linked to four others tetrahedrally | each carbon bonded to three others in a hexagonal net, giving three sigma bonds |
| Fourth valence electron | used in the fourth \(\mathrm{C-C}\) sigma bond | left in an unhybridised p orbital; these overlap laterally to form \(\pi\) bonds and the \(\pi\) electrons are delocalised over the whole layer |
| Structure | three dimensional network of strong \(\mathrm{C-C}\) single bonds | two dimensional sheets, held to one another only by weak van der Waals forces |
| \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond distance | 154 pm | 141.5 pm within a layer; layers separated by 335 pm |
| Hardness | the hardest natural substance | soft and slippery, because the layers slide over one another |
| Melting point | abnormally high, \(3930\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) | — the chapter gives no value |
| Electrical conduction | bad conductor of electricity | the delocalised \(\pi\) electrons make it a conductor |
| Stability | — | the thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon |
| Uses | cutting glass, drilling tools, dies for drawing thin wire, jewellery | — the chapter gives no list of uses |

Both are allotropes of phosphorus, described in section 9.6.2.

| | White (yellow) phosphorus | Red phosphorus |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | discrete tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecules | chains of \(\mathrm{P_4}\) tetrahedra linked together by covalent bonds, so it is polymeric |
| Appearance | translucent white waxy solid | possesses iron grey lustre |
| Glow in dark | it glows in dark (chemiluminescence) | it does not glow in dark |
| Odour | — | odourless |
| Solubility | insoluble in water but dissolves in boiling NaOH solution | insoluble in water |
| Toxicity | poisonous | non poisonous |
| Stability and reactivity | less stable and hence more reactive, because of the angular strain in the \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecule (the P-P-P bond angle is only \(60^\circ\)) | stable and less reactive |

The two are interconvertible: the 'Remember' box notes that red phosphorus is prepared by heating white phosphorus at 573 K in an inert atmosphere. Section 9.4.4 adds that phosphorus is stored under water because it catches fire when exposed to air.

**What they are.** Section 9.8.2 defines silicones as **organo-silicon polymers** in which \(\{\mathrm{R_2SiO}\}\) is the repeating unit, the chain being held together by \(-\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{Si}-\) linkages. Their empirical formula \(\mathrm{R_2SiO}\) (with R = \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) or \(\mathrm{C_6H_5}\)) is similar to that of a ketone \(\mathrm{(R_2CO)}\), and that resemblance is where the name *silicones* comes from.

**How they are made.** The starting materials are alkyl or aryl substituted silicon chlorides \(\mathrm{R_nSiCl_{(4-n)}}\). Methyl chloride reacts with silicon over a copper catalyst at 573 K to give the methyl-substituted chlorosilanes; hydrolysis of dimethyl dichlorosilane followed by condensation polymerisation then yields the straight-chain silicone polymer :

\(2\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{Si} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{Cu powder}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2}\)

\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{SiCl_2} \xrightarrow[-2\mathrm{HCl}]{2\mathrm{H_2O}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Si(OH)_2} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{polymerisation}} \left[-\mathrm{Si(CH_3)_2}-\mathrm{O}-\right]_n\)

The chain length is controlled by adding \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{SiCl}\), which caps the ends.

**Properties.** They are water repellant, have high thermal stability, are good electrical insulators, and are resistant to oxidation and chemicals.

**Where they are used.** The chapter lists five uses: as insulating material for electrical appliances; for water proofing of fabrics; as sealants; as high temperature lubricants; and for mixing in paints and enamels to make them resistant to high temperature, sunlight and chemicals.

Nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony and bismuth all have the outer electronic configuration \(n\mathrm{s}^2 n\mathrm{p}^3\), five valence electrons in all, so Table 9.5 gives their **group oxidation state as \(+5\)**, with \(+3\) and \(-3\) as the other states.

Section 9.4.1 gives the trend. In the nitrogen family the group oxidation state \(+5\) is the most stable state *for the lighter elements*; the lower states, two units below the group value, *become increasingly stable as we move down to heavier elements in the groups*. So on going from nitrogen to bismuth the \(+5\) state becomes progressively harder to reach and the \(+3\) state progressively more stable, until in bismuth \(+3\) is the characteristic state.

The 'Remember' box gives the cause — the **inert pair effect**. In the heavier members the two valence s-electrons are shielded poorly by the ten inner d-electrons, are therefore held more tightly by the nucleus, and take part less readily in chemical reactions; only the three p-electrons are used, which gives the \(+3\) state.

The chapter's own evidence for this runs across the group. Table 9.6 shows the corresponding oxides shifting from acidic \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) and \(\mathrm{P_2O_5}\), through amphoteric \(\mathrm{As_4O_6}\) and \(\mathrm{Sb_2O_3}\), to basic \(\mathrm{Bi_2O_3}\) — the higher oxides giving way to the lower ones. Section 9.4.4 adds that the trihalides of group 15 are predominantly covalent and that nitrogen is a special case at the top of the group: being a second-period element it has no d orbitals in its valence shell, so it cannot expand its octet and forms **no pentahalides at all**, as the worked example on \(\mathrm{NCl_5}\) and \(\mathrm{NF_5}\) explains.

[Textbook misprint: the question as printed reads 'to detect borate radical is qualitative analysis'; 'in qualitative analysis' is meant. Transcribed as printed; the answer is unaffected.]

Section 9.8.1 gives the test, and the 'Remember' box beside it states that *the above reaction is used as a test for detection and removal of borate in qualitative analysis*.

**The test.** The salt (a borate, here borax) is warmed with **ethyl alcohol and concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)**. Volatile vapours of **triethyl borate** are given off, and these **burn with a green edged flame** — the green edge is the positive test for the borate radical.

\(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} + 5\,\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} + 4\,\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)

\(\mathrm{H_3BO_3} + 3\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{B(OC_2H_5)_3} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The concentrated sulphuric acid liberates orthoboric acid from the borate, and the boric acid then esterifies with the alcohol to give the volatile triethyl borate \(\mathrm{B(OC_2H_5)_3}\). Because the borate leaves the mixture as a volatile ester, the same reaction also **removes** borate, which is why the chapter describes it as a test for detection *and removal*.

(The chapter also describes the **borax bead test** in the same section, but that one detects coloured transition metal ions in a borax bead — for example a blue \(\mathrm{Co(BO_2)_2}\) bead with CoO — rather than detecting the borate radical itself.)

Diborane is \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\). Section 9.7.4 explains why it cannot be written with ordinary two-electron bonds alone.

**The problem.** Boron has only three valence electrons. Two boron atoms and six hydrogen atoms supply \(2 \times 3 + 6 \times 1 = 12\) valence electrons in all, but six ordinary \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bonds would need twelve electrons *and* leave the two borons unjoined. Diborane is therefore **electron deficient**.

**The bonding.** Each boron atom is \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridised. Three of the four hybrid orbitals are half filled and the fourth is vacant.

- **Four terminal bonds.** Two half-filled \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) orbitals of each boron overlap with the 1s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms to give four ordinary \(\mathrm{B-H}\) covalent bonds. These four hydrogens are the *terminal* hydrogens.
- **Two bridge bonds.** For each of the remaining two hydrogen atoms, its 1s orbital overlaps **simultaneously** with a half-filled hybrid orbital of one boron and the **vacant** hybrid orbital of the other boron. Three atomic centres share a single electron pair, giving a **three centred - two electron (3c-2e) bond**, also called a **banana bond**. The two hydrogens involved are the *bridging* hydrogens.

**The shape.** The two boron atoms and the four terminal hydrogen atoms all lie in one plane; the two bridging hydrogen atoms lie symmetrically above and below that plane. The chapter's figure gives the terminal \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bond length as 119 pm and the bridge \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bond length as the longer 134 pm, with the \(\mathrm{H-B-H}\) angle \(120^\circ\) between the terminal hydrogens and \(97^\circ\) between the bridging ones. The longer bridge bond is the expected consequence of one electron pair being shared over three atoms rather than two.

The bonding and structure, as the chapter draws them, are shown with this answer.

The compound is **borax**, \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7}\) (sodium tetraborate).

Every clue in the question matches section 9.8.1. *Borax is prepared from the mineral colemanite by boiling it with a solution of sodium carbonate*; property (i) of the same section states that *borax is white crystalline solid*; and the section's list of uses includes its use in qualitative analysis for the borax bead test. Its crystalline form is \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7 \cdot 10H_2O}\), also written \(\mathrm{Na_2[B_4O_5(OH)_4] \cdot 8H_2O}\).

Section 9.8.1 gives the preparation. Colemanite, \(\mathrm{Ca_2B_6O_{11}}\), is boiled with a solution of sodium carbonate :

\(\mathrm{Ca_2B_6O_{11}} + 2\,\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7} + 2\,\mathrm{NaBO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{CaCO_3}\downarrow\)

The calcium is thrown out as insoluble calcium carbonate — the downward arrow marks the precipitate — and is filtered off, leaving the borax \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7}\) in solution together with sodium metaborate, from which the borax crystallises out as the white crystalline decahydrate \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7 \cdot 10H_2O}\).

Section 9.8.3, under 'Complex formation', gives the reason: *the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom facilitates complexation of ammonia with transition metal ions*.

In \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) the nitrogen uses three of its five valence electrons in the three \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bonds and keeps the remaining two as a **lone pair**. That lone pair can be donated whole into a vacant orbital of a metal ion, forming a coordinate bond — so ammonia acts as a **ligand** and the metal ion as the acceptor. Because ammonia is a small, neutral molecule with one such lone pair, several molecules can crowd around one metal ion, and the result is a complex ion.

The chapter gives two examples :

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 4\,\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4}]^{2\oplus}(aq)\) — **deep blue**

\(\mathrm{AgCl(s)} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]\mathrm{Cl(aq)}\) — **colourless**

The 'Remember' box notes that these reactions are used for the detection of metal ions such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\), and the section's list of uses accordingly includes aqueous ammonia as a laboratory reagent in qualitative and quantitative analysis. Note in the silver example that the complex is soluble while AgCl is not: complexation with ammonia dissolves a precipitate, which is exactly the behaviour the analysis relies on.

[Textbook misprint: the statement as printed reads 'down the graph' where 'down the group' is meant. Transcribed as printed; the statement is false either way.]

**False.**

Table 9.6 gives the nature of the stable oxides of group 13 down the group: \(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\) acidic, \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) amphoteric, \(\mathrm{Ga_2O_3}\) amphoteric, \(\mathrm{In_2O_3}\) basic and \(\mathrm{Tl_2O_3}\) basic. The acidic character therefore falls away going down the group, not increases. Section 9.4.3 states the same thing in words: the increase in metallic character down groups 13, 14 and 15 is reflected in their oxides, which *gradually vary from acidic through amphoteric to basic*.

**Corrected statement :** The acidic nature of oxides of group 13 **decreases** down the group.

[Textbook misprint: the question as printed spells catenation as 'cantenation'. Transcribed as printed; the chapter itself spells it catenation throughout section 9.5.]

**True.**

Section 9.5 defines catenation as the self-linking of atoms of an element by covalent bonds to form chains and rings, and states that *the catenation tendency of an element depends upon the strength of the bond formed*. It then gives the order for group 14 outright: \(\mathrm{C} \gg \mathrm{Si} > \mathrm{Ge} = \mathrm{Sn}\), with lead showing no catenation at all, and adds that *among the group 14 elements, carbon shows the maximum tendency for catenation because of the stronger \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond*.

The bond enthalpy table in the same section is the evidence: \(\mathrm{C-C}\) 348, \(\mathrm{Si-Si}\) 297, \(\mathrm{Ge-Ge}\) 260 and \(\mathrm{Sn-Sn}\) 240 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). The \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond is about 17 % stronger than \(\mathrm{Si-Si}\), so carbon chains are far more stable than silicon chains and carbon's catenation tendency is much the higher.

| A | B |
|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) | Planar trigonal molecule |
| \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) | Tetrahedral molecule |
| \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) | linear covalent molecule |

**\(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) — planar trigonal.** Section 9.7.1 states it directly: the boron atom is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised with one vacant unhybridised p orbital, and *the \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) is nonpolar trigonal plannar molecule*, the chapter's figure giving the \(\mathrm{Cl-B-Cl}\) angle as \(120^\circ\).

**\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) — tetrahedral.** Section 9.7.5 states that silicon dioxide is a covalent three dimensional network solid *in which each silicon atom is covalently bound in tetrahedral manner to four oxygen atoms*. Note that silica is a network solid rather than a set of discrete \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) molecules, so this entry describes the geometry around each silicon atom rather than the shape of a separate molecule.

**\(\mathrm{CO_2}\) — linear covalent molecule.** This is the remaining entry, and it is the correct one: carbon in \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms with no lone pair on the carbon, so the two bonds lie on opposite sides and the molecule is linear. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is listed among the stable compounds of group 14 in Table 9.5 and its oxide is called acidic in Table 9.6, but this chapter does not separately describe its shape.

**Angular molecule** is left unmatched — column B carries four entries against column A's three, so one is a distractor. None of the three species is angular: an angular (bent) shape needs one or more lone pairs on the central atom, and boron in \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\), silicon in \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) and carbon in \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) each have none.

Section 9.8.3, under 'Chemical properties', puts the basic nature first: *the aqueous solution of ammonia is basic in nature due to the formation of \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) ions*. The evidence is these reactions.

**1. With water — it produces hydroxide ions.**

\(\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

Ammonia accepts a proton from water using the lone pair on nitrogen, leaving \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) behind — the defining behaviour of a base.

**2. With acids — it forms ammonium salts.**

\(\mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

\(2\,\mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{SO_4}\)

Neutralising an acid to give a salt is base behaviour.

**3. With metal salt solutions — it precipitates metal hydroxides.**

\(\mathrm{ZnSO_4(aq)} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_4OH(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn(OH)_2(s)} + (\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{SO_4(aq)}\) — a white precipitate

\(\mathrm{FeCl_3(aq)} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_4OH(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl(aq)}\)

The aqueous solution of ammonia precipitates the hydroxides (or hydrated oxides) of metals out of their salt solutions, which it could only do by supplying \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) ions.

**What the observations mean.** Two tests were run in sequence and each narrows the answer.

- A **white precipitate on adding silver nitrate** tells Shravani that the salt contains a halide-type radical, since silver nitrate is the standard reagent for it and silver chloride is white.
- The precipitate then **dissolving in ammonium hydroxide to give a clear solution** is the confirming step. Section 9.8.3 gives exactly this reaction under complex formation — \(\mathrm{AgCl(s)} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]\mathrm{Cl(aq)}\), described there as **colourless** — and the 'Remember' box beside it states that this reaction is used for the detection of metal ions such as \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\). The lone pair on the nitrogen of ammonia is donated to the silver ion, giving the soluble diamminesilver(I) complex, and it is the solubility of that complex that redissolves the precipitate.

**Conclusion :** the salt is a **chloride** — it contains the chloride radical \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) — and the white precipitate was silver chloride.

**The reactions involved :**

\(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}(aq)} + \mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)}\downarrow + \mathrm{NO_3^{\ominus}(aq)}\)  (white precipitate)

\(\mathrm{AgCl(s)} + 2\,\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]\mathrm{Cl(aq)}\)  (clear, colourless solution)

The ammonia is supplied by the ammonium hydroxide she added, \(\mathrm{NH_4OH}\) being the aqueous solution of ammonia.
